🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +1.07% (intraday, 7-year -15bp). At trading day 33 (last close) it was +1.07% against a five-campaign average of -1.15% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -1.05%. The 10-year is -11bp since the hike vs a +14bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 780bp against a five-year average of 417bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +36bp and BB +20bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.41 → 0.65 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is moving too (+10bp in a month).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,110bp, +73bp since 2026-10-29, 85bp under the Oct 15 record and 658bp over the June low. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 80.5 (14.8%, -4.6pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 147bp, Oracle 301bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -38%, NBIS -34%, IREN -41% vs NVDA -11%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 18 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -15.1% vs -19.5% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 32% in 3m, 36% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 60%. Triggered signposts: Basket names >20% off high.
  • Bank Earnings: 1 bank reported (CBC); no red flags. Credit broadly stable; funding cost trend n/p.
  • Stocks: The Nasdaq fell about 1%, the Dow rose and the S&P slipped.
  • FX: The dollar eased slightly, and the euro and Swiss franc gained.
  • Technicals: The Nasdaq is barely above its long-term average and below its short-term average.
  • Sectors: Money left tech and energy for banks, consumer stocks and materials.
  • Credit/Spreads: Safer corporate bonds stay calm while stress in the junkiest debt stays high.
  • Crisis: Overall crisis risk looks moderate, with lower-quality and AI-related credit the weak points.
  • Inflation: Underlying inflation is stuck near 2.6–3.1%, and broad price pressure is not fading.
  • Tech Bubble: Tech is in an early sell-off with calm credit, and that phase usually lasts.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Apple (the biggest) and AppLovin (the biggest expected move) lead this week; IPO deals unconfirmed.
  • Iran: I could not verify any news from today; oil's fall is unexplained here.
  • Warsh: Warsh has leaned hawkish and avoided promises; a rate cut looks unlikely soon.
  • Week Ahead: Midterm elections, job openings data, Friday's jobs report and many Fed speakers.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term; protect against tech weakness and keep high-quality bonds.
  • Trades: Own Treasuries and high-grade credit; cut tech; avoid the weakest junk bonds.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 sell, 20 hold long, 24 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 0.4% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads widening
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.46 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 85th pctile, +39bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 0-10 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Oil Model: WTI $104.12 (2026-10-30). Oil model Base $105 / $93 / $83 at 3/6/12 months (Bull $99, Bear $67 at 12m), probability-weighted $83, against a futures strip of $95 / $90 / $81. Demand check: activity data imply +1.4 mb/d y/y against +0.7 from the GDP assumptions — worth a look.
  • Bottom line: A rotation, not a panic, but credit markets are flashing early warnings.

Monday's close was a rotation day, not a broad sell-off. Oil had the biggest move: WTI fell 7.72% to 96.08 and Brent fell 8.09% to 104.25. US Energy dropped 3.97% and Info Tech 2.66%. That pulled the Nasdaq down 1.07% to 25,164.32 and the S&P 500 down 0.51% to 7,541.40, while the Dow rose 0.41% to 51,983.98. Money moved into Cons Discr (+2.25%), Materials (+1.83%), Financials (+1.76%) and Staples (+1.75%). The VIX rose from 19.42 to 21.15. Gold gained 1.85% to 3,946.17 and long Treasury yields fell (10Y 4.9104%, 30Y 5.2857%). I could not verify a news cause for the oil drop (see Iran). Sentiment versus the prior session is defensive within equities, but the bond market is not panicking. Credit contagion (descriptive, not a signal). The extra yield on Caa bonds over single-B bonds is 781bp. That is the 99.6th percentile of the past five years, against a 5y average of 416bp, and it widened 242bp over 3 months. Some of the stress is now reaching single-B: B OAS is 335bp, +25bp over 1 month and +73bp over 3 months. Ba is +9bp over 1m and IG +7bp over 1m, so BB and investment grade are drifting wider but have not broken out. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose to 0.65 from 0.41 three months ago but is still below its 0.69 5y median. So the CCC rot is starting to touch single-B, but BB and IG are not yet following. AI backstop (descriptive). CoreWeave 5Y CDS rose 73bp since Oct 29 to about 1,110bp, 85bp below the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record. It still holds 89% of its run up from the June low. Nvidia 5Y CDS rose 17bp to 147bp, and Oracle (+24bp to 301bp) and Meta (+7bp) also widened. When the guarantor's own CDS widens alongside the neoclouds, the market is not fully buying Nvidia's backstop. Tech phase model. The basket is in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 18 days past its peak, with a basket drawdown of -15.09% versus -19.54% at the same point in 2000. One signpost has triggered: 57% of basket names are more than 20% below their highs, past the 50% trigger. The phase model gives a 0.412 chance of reaching Phase 2 or worse within 6 months.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 441.80 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 441.8 cents/gal, a 99.4th-percentile level with a 2.85 z-score, and all five gauges sit in their high zone at an extreme. The curve is in steep backwardation: 441.8 in the front month against 355.25 at month 12 and 273.41 at month 36. Together with a 4.63-z crack spread, that points to an acute shortage of prompt diesel and refining capacity rather than a broad repricing of long-dated supply. Each signal history favors mean reversion lower. The stops are very wide, though, which shows how violently these extremes can extend before they turn.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.46 vol points (10th percentile of the 58 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.4 (72th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 83bp (steeper by 3bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (125bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 32 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 60/100 — Inflation is sticky, not re-accelerating. The core trend measures (median, trimmed-mean and sticky) are mostly flat in the 2.3–2.8% range, and Median CPI is edging down. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score, shown separately, puts them in the upper-middle of their history. Core PCE at 3.12% is the outlier and keeps the Fed from easing. Breadth is the concern: in the Dallas distribution, 26.8% of the PCE basket is running above 5% and 16.6% above 10%, against 25.6% falling. Flexible CPI at 6.12% and rising reflects the energy shock. Today's 8% oil drop would ease that over time if it holds. Analyst estimate: persistence is moderate-to-high, and the path to 2% depends on energy, not on core improving.

BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 59/100
Today is clearly past a March-2000-style peak in price terms, though not in froth. Computed Equity Froth is far below 2000: Nasdaq trailing P/E is 39.83x against 175x (16% of peak conditions), the stretch over the 200DMA is 0.4% against 50% (1%), and SOX P/E is 36.56x against 60x (41%). Late-cycle catalysts are mixed. Credit tightness is beyond 2000 levels (IG 125%, Baa-10Y 157%), and the 2s10s curve is at 68%, but the ISM rollover readings are low (1% and 10%). In the macro regime, commodities vs equities scores 200% and the dollar 39%. Among bear-market signposts, financial conditions (152%) and VIX complacency (129%) are high, while sentiment is not euphoric: AAII is at 40% and consumer confidence at 31%. The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 18 days past the Day-0 peak of 2026-10-06. The basket is down 15.09% against -19.54% for the 2000 basket on the same day. The model puts 6-month odds at P1 0.535, P2 0.253, P3 0.111, P4 0.102, and the chance of ever reaching P2 or worse within 6 months at 0.412. At 12 months, P4 (trough/recovery) is 0.402. The breadth signpost has triggered (57% of names more than 20% off their highs). The HY, Baa and VIX signposts are moving toward their triggers but have not hit them. Rally watch: early warning, not armed. Note that today's VIX close of 21.15 is above the 20.2 spike line the panel computed on Oct 30 data.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

This looks like a valuation-light rerun of the 2000 bust's opening act. The froth that drove the 2000 crash, extreme P/Es and extreme price extension, is mostly absent. What rhymes is the combination of very easy credit and financial conditions, a crowded leadership group (semis and AI infrastructure), and early credit cracks at the edge of the AI stack. CoreWeave CDS is near its record, and Nvidia and Oracle CDS are widening. In 2000, Phase 1 often lasted months before credit confirmed. The model's 1m P1 odds of 0.833 say the same. The tell for moving to Phase 2 is HY OAS moving toward 420–448bp and Baa-10Y toward 195bp, not the Nasdaq's daily moves. The five numbers concentration_today (about 40%), ipo_froth_pct (55), CAPE (about 38x), Buffett ratio (about 210%) and lt_eps_growth_pct (60) are analyst estimates. They were not web-verified this run because the search budget went to Iran/Warsh/calendar, so treat them as approximate.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 6%; within two weeks: 10%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 50% later fail below their starting low (median 18 trading days, +11%); the rest become recoveries (median 106 days, +32%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: a hold with hawkish language at the next FOMC (date not verified here). Warsh rejects forward guidance, reaffirmed the 2% target, and at Sintra pushed back on the case for cuts without ruling out hikes. With Core PCE at 3.12% and the US 2Y at 4.5937%, a cut is unlikely. A hike is possible if core stays above 3%. I could not verify the September/October 2026 decisions or the current target range.

~1 YEAR

Inference: over about a year, expect a smaller Fed balance sheet (a priority he signaled at his Senate hearing), less forward guidance and more meeting-by-meeting decisions, and an overhaul of Fed operations. Rate cuts would likely come only if the labor market cracks; NFP was 29k, unemployment 4.2%, and the Sahm rule reads 0.0. Balance-sheet runoff with steady policy rates would tend to support a steeper curve over time.

On the record: Warsh's first meeting as chair in June held rates at 3.5%–3.75% unanimously, he declined to submit a dot, and nine officials projected at least one hike this year (PBS, Fortune). He has argued forward guidance limits Fed flexibility, sought an overhaul of Fed operations (The National), and flagged the balance sheet in his confirmation hearing (Fortune, Apr 21). His Sintra appearance was read as hawkish (TMGM analysis). Everything after July 2026 is inference: I found no verified coverage of later meetings. Note that the 2Y yield (4.59%) sits well above the June range, which implies either later hikes or a market pricing them. I am not asserting which.

Sources: PBS NewsHour — What Warsh's first meeting as Fed chair signals · Fortune — How did the market react to Kevin Warsh's press conference (Jun 17, 2026) · The National — Kevin Warsh seeks overhaul of Federal Reserve operations · Fortune — Warsh-era Fed balance sheet, inflation: Senate committee hearing (Apr 21, 2026) · TMGM — What did Kevin Warsh say in his first international appearance?

Descriptive regime read, not advice and not a recommendation to trade. Rule results are simulations on one market history (3x daily returns rebuilt from index data, 1-day lag, costs), and the exits (+10% target, 5-day pause) were chosen after testing a few values on that same history, so treat them as in-sample. The trend+vol engine is a drawdown control, not proven timing skill (trendvol TRENDVOL.md § CORRECTION). Credit widening = 63-day change past the monitor_spread triggers (Baa +0.15pp, HY OAS +0.50pp, IG OAS +0.15pp); as a standalone overlay that rule failed its pre-registered gates. Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily and decay.
